title: Threat Model and Spectrum Recon
scenario: A smart tolling corridor receives ETA and toll telemetry from passing vehicles. The operator assumed the air interface was private because it was not published.
objective: Inspect the waterfall and explain the first contested-spectrum principle: anyone in range can observe transmissions.
signal_scheme: C01 OOK/ASK passive recon: a fixed low-duty roadside beacon plus a weak neighbouring burst, designed to teach visibility before exploitation.
steps: Open the waterfall and identify the repeating burst pattern.
Measure whether bursts appear at a predictable interval.
Decide what the threat model must assume about nearby listeners.
Submit the principle as a flag.
hints: Look for vertical energy spikes that repeat over time.
The task is not asking you to break encryption yet. It is asking who can observe.
The sketch phrase 'ALL can listen' is very close to the flag.

title: Find the Scheme
scenario: The tolling unit emits short telemetry bursts near the toll gantry. The capture contains a simple teaching modulation rather than a real tolling standard.
objective: Use the artifact metadata and waterfall to identify the channel, burst timing, modulation family, and vehicle identifier.
signal_scheme: C02 2-FSK hop-set discovery: a fixed pilot and a five-channel hopping telemetry burst used to recover VH-7A29.
steps: Download the SigMF metadata and inspect the centre frequency and sample rate.
Use the waterfall to locate the active offset from centre.
Identify the simple on-off keyed burst shape.
Recover the training vehicle ID used by later backend tasks.
hints: SigMF metadata is plain JSON. Start there before touching DSP tooling.
The teaching signal is OOK/ASK-like: energy present means one state, energy absent means another.
The recovered vehicle ID is VH-7A29.

title: Decode the Toll Request
scenario: A decoded RF frame appears to carry enough backend parameters to request a toll quote.
objective: Read the simplified telemetry payload and identify why the checksum is not a real authentication mechanism.
signal_scheme: C03 BPSK framed request: visible preamble, payload body, and checksum trailer blocks that map onto decoded toll fields.
steps: Open the decoded packet notes.
Extract vehicle ID, booth ID, timestamp, route, schedule, and checksum.
Notice that the checksum is only a short additive training checksum.
Submit the checksum weakness flag.
hints: A checksum can detect accidental corruption without proving who sent the packet.
Replayable fields are dangerous if the backend trusts them directly.
The training checksum secret is written in the decoded notes.

title: Backend Recon
scenario: The web toll API accepts vehicle IDs recovered from the RF capture. One training endpoint builds SQL unsafely so you can study injection and the correct defence.
objective: Use the local API console to trigger an SQL error, enumerate schema details, and find the toll schedule table.
signal_scheme: C04 CSS/LoRa-like uplink bridge: the recovered RF identifier becomes the backend query parameter, where SQLi begins.
steps: Query the vulnerable events endpoint with vehicle_id=VH-7A29.
Append a quote to trigger a visible SQL error.
Use a UNION payload against sqlite_master to enumerate tables.
Find the schedules table and submit the recon flag.
hints: SQLite stores schema information in sqlite_master.
The vulnerable endpoint returns five columns: event_id, vehicle_id, booth_id, route_code, schedule_code.
A useful training payload is ' UNION SELECT name,type,sql,'x','x' FROM sqlite_master--

title: Free Trip Logic Flaw
scenario: The toll quote service trusts a schedule code from telemetry. Your goal is to get a zero-dollar trip without being an operator.
objective: Combine recovered RF parameters with backend behaviour to request a schedule that prices the trip at zero.
signal_scheme: C05 GFSK replay logic trace: an original STANDARD burst and a delayed drifting replay echo carrying MAINT_FREE.
steps: Use the recovered vehicle, booth, and route fields.
Discover the special zero-price schedule through recon.
Request a quote using that schedule code.
Submit the flag returned by the quote service.
hints: The endpoint should not trust schedule_code just because it appeared in telemetry.
Look for a schedule that was intended for maintenance/test traffic.
The vulnerable quote endpoint returns the flag only when price is zero.

title: Reverse the Decoder
scenario: A recovered roadside maintenance utility decodes SFCTF telemetry frames. The source-backed artifact mirrors the local binary challenge path for systems where a compiler is not available.
objective: Reverse the frame format, identify the weak checksum boundary, and recover the decoder flag.
signal_scheme: C06 Manchester-coded maintenance frame: timing transitions and a checksum trailer drive the decoder reverse-engineering task.
steps: Open the telemetry frame artifact and identify the delimiter and magic/version field.
Inspect or run the decoder tool to map each field to its meaning.
Determine which fields are covered by the weak checksum.
Recover the flag emitted by the decoder when the checksum validates.
hints: The frame starts with a magic/version field.
The checksum is not cryptographic; it is just a byte-sized additive teaching checksum.
Run the Python decoder against artifacts/telemetry-frame.txt if you want the fastest verification path.

title: Parser Panic
scenario: A synthetic roadside parser copies telemetry fields into fixed-size buffers. The unsafe version represents the class of memory-safety mistakes that serious RF/cyber systems must eliminate.
objective: Compare the vulnerable and safe parser sources, explain the memory-safety flaw, and trigger or reason about the controlled local success condition.
signal_scheme: C07 AFSK long-field burst: a malformed VHF-style callsign field becomes parser input and reaches the stack-copy bug.
steps: Read the vulnerable parser source and identify the unsafe copy operation.
Compare it to the safe parser source and its length checks.
Use the oversized sample frame as the local training input.
Submit the flag associated with the controlled parser success condition.
hints: The vulnerable source uses strcpy into fixed-size stack fields.
The safe version rejects fields that exceed their destination buffer.
This challenge is local-only and synthetic; the flag string is visible in the vulnerable source for source-backed environments.

title: Waveform Protocol RE
scenario: The signal is no longer just a visible burst. The player must infer framing behaviour from hop timing, preamble, sync word, whitening, and field boundaries.
objective: Reverse the RF-side framing notes enough to recover the preamble, sync word, hop set, whitening seed, and frame field order.
signal_scheme: C08 DSSS-over-FHSS waveform RE: a widened spread payload rides a hop schedule with explicit sync and whitening artefacts.
steps: Open the annotated contested waterfall and identify the hop-set timing.
Use the radio intercept artifact to recover preamble and sync word values.
Inspect the waveform notes to identify whitening seed and field order.
Explain which fields become backend input after demodulation.
Submit the waveform reverse-engineering flag.
hints: The hop set is visible as discrete active channels, not a continuous sweep.
The preamble and sync word are in the intercept metadata because this is still source-backed training.
Whitening hides long runs; it does not authenticate a frame.

title: Firmware Keyhunt
scenario: A synthetic roadside-unit firmware bundle contains debug strings, a command table, and a training key derivation path. The goal is reverse engineering, not real device exploitation.
objective: Reverse the firmware manifest and source-backed image notes to find the hidden diagnostic command and explain why hard-coded secrets are unacceptable.
signal_scheme: C09 maintenance diagnostic sideband: a narrowband FSK service channel leaks command names that line up with firmware strings.
steps: Open the firmware manifest and identify architecture, memory map, and enabled hardening notes.
Inspect the synthetic strings dump for diagnostic command names.
Find the command table entry that unlocks the training flag path.
Contrast this with the secure-mode requirement: signed firmware, protected keys, and attestation.
Submit the firmware RE flag.
hints: Start with strings before deeper reversing.
Diagnostic interfaces become dangerous when they survive into deployed builds.
The flag is tied to a maintenance command that should require signed firmware and device attestation.

title: Length Field Chaos
scenario: A second synthetic parser accepts binary-ish telemetry frames with nested TLVs. It has a length-field mismatch that models a common protocol parser bug class.
objective: Compare vulnerable and safe TLV parser sources, identify the integer/length mismatch, and use the malicious sample to reach the controlled flag path.
signal_scheme: C10 4-FSK malformed TLV burst: header cadence and an oversized value block feed the length-field parser bug.
steps: Read the vulnerable TLV parser and identify where declared length and available buffer length diverge.
Open the malicious TLV sample and locate the oversized nested operator note.
Compare against the safe parser and its checked arithmetic.
Describe how fuzzing would generate this class of input.
Submit the length-field exploit flag.
hints: Look for arithmetic on untrusted length fields before copying.
A parser can be SQLi-safe and cryptographically aware while still memory-unsafe.
The flag string is present in the vulnerable source for source-backed training.

title: RF-to-Operator XSS Sink
scenario: Decoded RF note fields are displayed in an operator console. Attack Mode renders one decoded note as HTML, turning RF-origin text into a browser execution sink.
objective: Receive an AFSK-style operator-note burst, post the decoded note, and see why RF-derived strings must be output-encoded before browser rendering.
signal_scheme: C11 AFSK operator-note telemetry: a decoded note field crosses from RF analysis into an operator web console, demonstrating the sink.
steps: Open the operator console in Attack Mode.
Use Receive RF burst to decode the current radio intercept into operational fields.
Post the decoded event with its RF-origin operator_note field.
Observe that the unsafe renderer treats the decoded note as markup.
Switch to Secure Mode and observe that the same RF-origin note is escaped/rendered as text.
hints: The sink is not the RF demodulator; it is the browser console rendering a decoded RF string unsafely.
A harmless local payload proves the trust-boundary failure without exfiltration.
Secure Mode demonstrates output encoding and safe DOM rendering for the exact same decoded note.

title: Propagation and Jamming Analysis
scenario: The range now contains a fixed roadside beacon, hopping telemetry, a drifting replay echo, a sweep interferer, and a protocol-aware noise-band jammer.
objective: Use the annotated waterfall with frequency/time zoom to classify the interference type and identify which signal is operationally suspicious rather than merely loud.
signal_scheme: C12 propagation/jamming scene: FHSS telemetry, replay drift, sweep interference, and protocol-aware noise-band jamming coexist.
steps: Open the annotated waterfall artifact and zoom the frequency axis around the hop set.
Use the time zoom to compare the fixed beacon cadence, hopper cadence, and replay echo delay.
Identify the sweep interferer and the wideband noise-band jammer as distinct behaviours.
Explain why the drifting replay echo is a cyber-physical threat even when it is weaker than the jammer.
Submit the propagation/jamming classification flag.
hints: The loudest signal is not always the most security-relevant signal.
Sweep interference moves across frequency; replay tends to preserve protocol timing but may show oscillator drift or stale nonce behaviour.
The expected answer combines jamming classification with replay awareness.

title: SOTA Range Assurance
scenario: A serious contested-spectrum system cannot rely on a single control. RF resilience, hardware trust, protocol security, backend policy, and detection all have to agree.
objective: Design a layered assurance plan for the tolling range that would survive valid-looking telemetry, hostile RF conditions, compromised tooling, and backend abuse.
signal_scheme: C13 SOTA fusion scenario: adaptive control hops, attested-device heartbeat, suspicious valid packets, and null-steering markers.
steps: Start from Secure Mode and list what it already fixes: HMAC, freshness, replay cache, safe SQL, and server-side authorization.
Add hardware controls: secure boot, signed firmware, protected keys, measured boot, and remote attestation for roadside units.
Add RF controls: adaptive hopping, coding/interleaving, directional receive, interference classification, holdover rules, and propagation-aware thresholds.
Add cyber controls: memory-safe parsing, fuzzing, compiler hardening, CSP/output encoding, least privilege, and policy enforcement.
Add detection controls that fuse RF features with decoded protocol state and backend logs.
Submit the layered assurance flag.
hints: Safe SQL does not prove the RF packet is fresh or physically plausible.
A valid HMAC does not prove the device booted trusted firmware or that the operator console is safe.
The hard-level answer needs hardware, RF, protocol, backend, binary-safety, and detection layers.

title: Contested Spectrum Defence
scenario: After finding passive collection, replay, weak integrity, SQLi, and logic abuse, propose the defensive design for the tolling range.
objective: Select mitigations that address both the RF and backend failures.
signal_scheme: C14 clean-vs-contested defence trace: clean FHSS telemetry transitions into spot jamming, sweep jamming, and replay pressure.
steps: Compare clean telemetry with replayed/jammed observations.
Choose RF mitigations that reduce simple collection or disruption.
Choose cyber mitigations that stop replay, SQLi, and logic abuse.
Submit the combined defence flag.

artifacts.label: C14 clean vs jammed defence capture

hints: Frequency hopping alone does not fix a backend SQL injection.
Prepared statements alone do not prove a packet is fresh.
The expected set includes hopping, nonces/timestamps, signed messages, backend validation, and anomaly detection.
